blocks.text: Port Coquitlam Lots and Land: streets and boundaries

items.t: This page covers the whole City of Port Coquitlam, between the Coquitlam River on the west and the Pitt River on the east, with Lougheed Highway (Highway 7) and the Mary Hill Bypass (Highway 7B) crossing it and Shaughnessy Street and Coast Meridian Road as the main north–south routes.

The plan frame is the Official Community Plan (OCP) Bylaw No. 3838, which identifies Downtown as a mixed-use neighbourhood and sets the development permit areas, including watercourse protection, that overlay the city's lots.

Low land is a defining fact of this city's lot fabric: a significant portion of Port Coquitlam is within the Fraser and Pitt River floodplain and is protected by dyke infrastructure, with pump stations and dyke patrols.

Agricultural Land Reserve (ALR) land sits in the south of the city, including land in and around Colony Farm Regional Park at the west edge of the central area — a land page for this city cannot treat every open parcel as development land.

blocks.text: Port Coquitlam Lots and Land: the housing stock

items.t: The redevelopment form of the land is set by the apartment zones: RA1 allows a floor area ratio (FAR, floor area divided by lot area) of 1.0, increasable to 1.5 where required parking is underground or in a structure and further to 2.0 on payment of a $50 per square foot contribution to City reserve funds for community amenities, and RA2 allows FAR up to 2.5, both concentrated downtown and along main roads.
Minimum lot widths for detached lots are zone-specific: RS1 requires at least 15 metres, RS2 at least 12 metres, RS3 at least 30 metres and RS4 at least 9.5 metres, under Zoning Bylaw No. 3630.

blocks.text: Port Coquitlam Lots and Land: rules that affect buyers

items.t: Small-scale multi-unit housing (SSMUH) changes what a house lot can hold without rezoning: RS-zoned lots across the city can hold 3 to 6 units depending on lot size, location and transit proximity, with an accessory dwelling unit capped at 90 square metres and a secondary suite capped at 40% of the principal unit's floor area in the City's amendment summary.

A watercourse permit can come before a subdivision: in the OCP's Watercourse Protection Development Permit areas, no filling, alteration or damage to a watercourse, ditch or adjacent environmentally sensitive land can occur without a Watercourse Development Permit, and subdivision is one of the activities that requires it.

Trees on a vacant lot are permit-controlled: the Tree Bylaw, 2019, No. 4108 lets the City issue a tree cutting permit with conditions on the extent, timing and replacement of cutting, and refuse one where cutting would fall in the active nesting season without a biological survey.

Flood position is checked lot by lot, not by neighbourhood: parts of the low city sit behind the Pitt River dike system, and flood status and any flood construction requirement are confirmed with the City for the specific parcel.

blocks.text: Port Coquitlam Lots and Land: local details a buyer would not know

items.t: The City's development application fees are charged per lot on a sliding scale for residential subdivision: the first 20 lots are charged per proposed lot at the higher rate, lots 21 to 60 at a lower rate, and remaining lots at the lowest rate, under the Fees and Charges Bylaw.

A Watercourse Development Permit is cheap on paper but not in work: the City's 2026 fees schedule charges $500 for the permit in agricultural and residential small-scale zones, and the application itself requires an environmental study prepared by a qualified professional.

The current fees bylaw is Fees and Charges Bylaw, 2025, No. 4415, in effect January 1, 2026, and its Schedule K is the Subdivision and Engineering Development schedule — the schedule a land buyer prices from.
Utility charges for a Port Coquitlam lot are flat annual water and sewer fees, billed separately from taxes and due March 31, 2026 — a vacant lot still sits inside that billing cycle.
There is no SkyTrain in Port Coquitlam to price into a lot: an extension is an exploratory business case only in the Mayors' Council February 19, 2026 work plan, with no funding, route or dates.

blocks.text: Port Coquitlam Lots and Land: development and new projects

items.t: Cedar Drainage Pump Station rebuild, Cedar Drive near Chelsea Avenue, City of Port Coquitlam capital project inside the dike system at the northeast end of the city: construction scheduled summer 2026 to summer 2027, completion expected late summer 2027 — status: under construction window (as of November 3, 2026).

blocks.text: Port Coquitlam Lots and Land: costs and taxes

items.t: Proposed Parks DCC rate for a new single-family lot: $15,253 per dwelling unit or lot, city-wide, in the draft rates the City presented to Council on July 8, 2025 — proposed, not yet the in-force rate.
Utility DCC rates sit in the City's Development Cost Charge Bylaw 2023, No. 4320, as footnoted in the City's own Parks DCC engagement material.

Permit fees a land buyer meets: a Watercourse Development Permit costs $500 in agricultural and residential small-scale zones and $2,500 in commercial, industrial, institutional, rowhouse, townhouse, apartment and comprehensive development zones, under Fees and Charges Bylaw, 2025, No. 4415.
Tax timing on a held lot: 2026 property taxes were due July 2, 2026, the City's 2026 increase was 1.95% for the average home, and utility bills are flat annual fees due March 31, 2026.

blocks.text: Port Coquitlam Lots and Land: getting around

items.t: The West Coast Express stops at Port Coquitlam Station, between Coquitlam Central Station and Pitt Meadows Station, on the line between Waterfront Station and Mission City — the commuter rail fact for this city's lots.

The R3 Lougheed Hwy RapidBus runs along Lougheed Highway through the city, and TransLink buses connect Port Coquitlam to Coquitlam Central Station on the Millennium Line Evergreen Extension; there is no SkyTrain station inside the city.

blocks.text: Port Coquitlam Lots and Land: risks and due diligence

items.t: Check the floodplain and dike position for the specific lot with the City first: a significant portion of the city is in the Fraser and Pitt River floodplain behind dikes, and the City page does not give a lot-level flood construction level.

Check the Watercourse Protection Development Permit layer in OCP Bylaw No. 3838 for any lot with a creek, ditch or slough: Hyde Creek and DeBoville Slough drain the city's low ground into the Pitt River, and the permit layer, not the street address, decides whether an environmental study is required.
Check Agricultural Land Reserve status per parcel on the Agricultural Land Commission mapping, especially south-city and Colony Farm edge parcels; a view over the ALR is not ALR status.
4108 permit conditions can set the extent, timing and replacement planting for any clearing.
